Hook

Top hooks, yt-script score

  • 0Two twenty-somethings in Miami beach flats won a 300 million dollar contract to arm Afghanistan. One was a massage therapist.
  • 0At 18 he had 1.8 million dollars from selling to the US military, from a laptop in a one-room flat.

Look and device

Running device

A government contract ledger that fills line by line with a big running dollar counter, and a split screen: sunny Miami penthouse on one side, dusty Afghan airstrip on the other.

Look

Crime-caper explainer in the house 2D style, Leo sheet style characters. Painted plates: a Miami synagogue courtyard and basketball court, an LA police-supply warehouse, a tiny one-room Miami flat lit by a laptop, a Paris arms-fair hall, a Miami Beach high-rise pool, a US Army office at Rock Island, maps of Eastern Europe and Afghanistan. Turquoise and pink Miami against khaki and olive war colours. Real people stylised with no likeness; Bush and the 9/11 attacks shown only as a TV news screen with text, no likeness and no attack imagery. Drug use only implied (smoke cloud, 'baked' joke card), never shown in detail. SFX under the VO (phone rings, keyboard, cash register, jet engines), music at combine.

Act 1: The Teenage Gun Salesman

0:49 · 5 shots · 120 words
  1. 1.01WIDE9.8s

    Efraim Diveroli grows up in a strict Orthodox Jewish family in Miami. Guns run in the family: an uncle sells weapons to police departments.

    A Miami family home; a framed photo of an uncle beside a gun-shop sign.

    EFRAIM DIVEROLI

    ANIMATIONBoy looks up at the sign.

  2. 1.02MED10.2s

    He's a wild kid. He drinks, skips school and gets expelled at 14. His parents send him to Los Angeles to live with that uncle.

    A school gate slams; a boy with a suitcase at an airport.

    EXPELLED AT 14

    ANIMATIONGate slams; he walks off.

  3. 1.03MED9.8s

    He starts in the warehouse, stacking boxes. Then September 11th, 2001. America goes to war in Afghanistan, then Iraq, and the arms business booms.

    A warehouse; a TV in the corner showing a news ticker: WAR ON TERROR.

    2001

    ANIMATIONTicker scrolls; boxes stack higher.

  4. 1.04MED7.9s

    At 16 he's selling guns over the phone to police departments. Nobody on the line knows he's a teenager.

    A teen at a desk on the phone; a cop on the other side of a split screen.

    AGE 16

    ANIMATIONPhone cord bounces; cop nods.

  5. 1.05MED11.3s

    He fights with his uncle over money he says he's owed, about 75,000 dollars. So he flies home to Miami, taking a pile of client files with him.

    Two figures arguing; then the teen on a plane hugging a stack of folders.

    $75,000

    ANIMATIONFolders slide into a bag.

Act 2: A Laptop and a Website

1:00 · 5 shots · 148 words
  1. 2.01MED11.7s

    Back in Miami he takes over a dormant company his father owned, called AEY, so it looks like an established business. He's too young to hold the licences himself.

    A dusty company sign 'AEY INC.' gets wiped clean.

    AEY, INC.

    ANIMATIONDust wipes off the sign.

  2. 2.02MED9.8s

    His office is a one-room flat. His tool is a public government website called FedBizOpps, where the military posts what it wants to buy.

    A tiny flat with a laptop glowing; the website's listing scrolls.

    FEDBIZOPPS

    ANIMATIONListings scroll: helmets, toilet seats, rockets.

  3. 2.03MED13.6s

    Anything from toilet seats to rocket launchers. Here's the game. The Army wants 20,000 helmets. You find a factory that sells them for 2.2 million, add shipping, bid 2.7 million, and keep the difference.

    A ledger: helmets $2.2M + shipping $0.3M, bid $2.7M; a gap labelled PROFIT.

    BID $2.7M

    ANIMATIONBars stack; profit slice glows.

  4. 2.04MED13.9s

    The trick is to bid lower than everyone else. On the phone he can sound like a gruff ex-Marine. In 2004, by his own count, he wins over a million dollars of contracts. He's 18.

    The teen in a fake moustache on the phone; contract papers flying in.

    AGE 18

    ANIMATIONPapers flutter onto the desk.

  5. 2.05MED10.6s

    Bigger deals need cash up front. A Utah businessman in his sixties, Ralph Merrill, agrees to put up the money in return for half the profits.

    An older man in a suit opening a briefcase of cash; a handshake.

    THE BACKER

    ANIMATIONHandshake; briefcase clicks shut.

Fact log

Fixes against the transcript

  • Afghan ammunition contract awarded January 2007, worth up to about $298M (source 'almost $300M').
  • Diveroli born December 1985; age claims ('at 16 selling', '$1.8M at 18-19') are his and Packouz's own accounts, worded as such.
  • AEY was his father's shell company; kept as 'a dormant company his father owned'.
  • Nepal deal kept short and neutral; no claim on outcome.
  • Albania stockpile figure attributed to UN estimates.
  • Bid gap $52M per Packouz/Lawson.
  • Bush, 9/11 shown only as a TV ticker, no likeness or attack imagery.

Removed from the transcript

  • Brilliant sponsor read removed.
  • Channel narrator-change notes cut.
  • Drug details reduced to one line.
  • Film comparisons (Jonah Hill, Bradley Cooper) cut.
  • Rewritten in our own words.
